tectonic-processes-and-hazards: The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
After a 2004 earthquake off Sumatra, people died in 10 countries around the Indian Ocean. How?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
In one Aceh village, the 2004 tsunami killed four females for every male. Why would a wave "choose"?
About 1,600 magnitude-5 earthquakes strike each year, and about one magnitude-8. Which should planners prepare for?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?
A modest eruption in Iceland grounded flights across Europe. What turns a disaster into a global one?
Large earthquakes are not becoming more common. So why do experts expect more people to be affected by geophysical disasters?
By 2013, Hong Kong said it had cut the landslide risk from its man-made slopes by about 75%. Is preventing disasters worth more than responding to them?
glaciated-landscapes-and-change: Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice are up to 800,000 years old. What can they tell us about past climate?
Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
Near Tuktoyaktuk in Arctic Canada, a 49 m hill rises out of flat tundra. Its core is solid ice. How did it form?
Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
Some glaciers race forward metres a day. Others, frozen to their beds, barely move. Why the difference?
Yosemite's Lembert Dome has a gentle slope on one side and a steep face on the other. Why?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
How can a ridge of river gravel wind uphill and over hills, when rivers only flow downhill?
Glaciated landscapes power cities, feed herds and draw pilgrims. Should they be used, or left alone?
Yosemite Valley draws millions of visitors, yet most of the park is legal wilderness. How can both work?
Shishmaref, an Iñupiaq village on an Alaskan island, has voted three times to move. Why, and why is it still there?
coastal-landscapes-and-change: Some coasts are chains of long islands; others, headlands and bays. Why do coasts take such different shapes?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
Bare, sticky mud is flooded by tide after tide. How does it turn into a meadow that cattle can graze?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
A Dorset cliff retreats only centimetres a year on average, yet can lose twenty metres in a few slides. How?
On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises out of the sea by about 0.9 m a century. Elsewhere, coasts are drowning. How can both be true?
A dam is built hundreds of kilometres inland. How could it make a coastline vanish?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?
Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
1,282 people and organisations sent formal comments on one plan for the Suffolk coast. Who were they, and who won?
globalisation: In 2023 the Panama Canal cut the number of ships it let through. In 2026 conflict choked oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Has technology really made the world "shrink"?
From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?
In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
The Netherlands tops the KOF Globalisation Index. The USA, the world's largest economy at market exchange rates, ranks 28th. How can that be?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
In 2006, more than a third of China's sulfur dioxide emissions came from making goods for other countries. Whose pollution is it?
Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
regenerating-places: Men in Wokingham live about nine years longer than men in Blackpool. What has work got to do with it?
Is a place just a dot on a map, or something more?
Your street has a story no map tells. How do you uncover what made your own place what it is?
A poet begged bombs to fall on a town. Can a poem change how a real place is seen and treated?
Santa Clara County, in Silicon Valley, has a median household income about twice the US figure. Could any part of it need regeneration?
In one London borough, one ward's turnout was more than double another's. Why do some people engage less?
Britain is backing a new railway and a new runway. Will they spread wealth beyond London?
How does a place with closed factories persuade investors and visitors to come?
A million visitors a year come to one small stretch of coast. Is that regeneration or a problem?
Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017. Years later, how could anyone prove whether it worked?
Two neighbourhoods on two continents: both were demolished and redeveloped. Who decides what replaces a neighbourhood?
diverse-places: Since 1981 London has added over two million people. Why has the North East barely grown?
Why would migrants choose a small market town in the Lincolnshire fens over a big city?
Victorian London was feared as dangerous. Why do so many young adults now choose to live there?
Why do some people dream of moving to a village while teenagers can't wait to leave?
18.5 million people born in India live in other countries, more than from any other country. How do they change places at both ends?
Why do some migrant communities cluster in the poorest neighbourhoods, and do their grandchildren stay?
When a place changes fast, why do some residents welcome it while others push back?
Survey estimates show a town with 3,000 more people in work, yet a lower employment rate. Is it doing better or worse?
Rioting among young people led a town to found a youth-run peace charity. How would you judge if it worked?
Nearly a third of homes in England's largest national park are not lived in all year. Who is the park for?
the-water-cycle-and-water-insecurity: At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
In December 2023 the Panama Canal let through 22 ships a day, against 36 in its "regular scenario". What did a patch of warm Pacific Ocean have to do with it?
A study found that urbanisation made Hurricane Harvey-scale flooding in Houston's basins about 21 times as likely in 2017. How can a city make a flood worse?
Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?
In January 2018 Cape Town, a city of just over 4 million people, warned that its taps could be turned off in April: "Day Zero". What pushed it to the edge, and how did it pull back?
Producing 1 kg of beef takes about 15,400 litres of water, on a world average. Is beef draining the world's rivers?
About 85% of the Nile's water starts in Ethiopia, yet a 1959 agreement shared it between Egypt and Sudan. Who decides how it is used now, and what would make a deal work?

The Lower Mekong's fisheries land an estimated 2.3 million tonnes of fish a year, worth about US$11 billion. Its hydropower capacity could more than double. Can one river be both a great fishery and a giant power station?

Singapore imports more than 90% of its food and makes about 95% of its electricity from imported gas. Jordan has about 61 m³ of renewable water per person a year. Which is more resource-secure, and why?
the-carbon-cycle-and-energy-security: Most of Earth's carbon is locked away in rock. How does any of it get back into the air?
The ocean took up 29% of the CO₂ humans emitted over the last decade. Why is that bad news for coral reefs?
In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
In 2025, solar power generation grew by about 30%. In the same year, the world used more fossil fuel than ever. How can both be true?

In March, April and May 2026, oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 2.7 million barrels a day, down from about 20 million. Why did farmers and food importers far from the Gulf feel the shock?
Some oil and gas now come from sticky sand, cracked rock or far beneath the seabed. Is it worth the cost?
Britain once made almost three-quarters of its electricity from coal. What replaced it, and at what cost?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?
Clear the Amazon's trees and the streams run fuller. So why could the region end up drier?
Clearing tropical forest and savanna brings farms, jobs and food. Who gains, and what is lost?
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times as fast as the planet as a whole. Why there?
The least developed countries emitted less than 0.4% of all historical fossil CO₂, yet face some of the worst impacts. Who should cut emissions, and who should pay?
superpowers: In 2025 China's economy was larger than the USA's by one IMF measure and smaller by another. Which country is the superpower?
Ruling colonies directly, or pulling strings from afar: which kind of power keeps the world stable?
China emits a third of the world's carbon dioxide; Brazil hosted COP30. Are emerging powers taking charge?
In 1980 the G7 produced about half the world's output (IMF, at PPP). By 2025 it produced under 30%. Do the old clubs still run the world economy?
China now files more international patents than the USA. Why does the USA still earn far more from ideas?
The USA has left the Paris climate deal twice. China never left. Which superpower is doing more for the climate?
Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognise their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?
In 2024, ships from Shenzhen to Rotterdam began sailing about 3,000 extra nautical miles around Africa. Why take the long way?
China buys Africa's copper and oil and sells it machines and cars. Who gains most from the deal?
One narrow strait carried oil equal to about a fifth of world consumption. Why can no great power ignore the Middle East?
Can the USA and the EU afford to stay on top of the world until 2050?
health-human-rights-and-intervention: A small country tops a world wellbeing league, while far richer nations rank low. So what should development mean?
In 2000, non-communicable diseases caused 58% of the world's deaths. In 2023 they caused 74%. Good news or bad news?
In 2022 Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt and turned to the IMF. Who sets the terms of rescue loans, and is there an alternative?
Forty-eight countries voted for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Did that bind any of them?
In 2025 Access Now recorded at least 313 internet shutdowns. Can citizens win back the freedom to connect?
Nearly half of the 2.4 million elected members of India's rural local councils are women. Can reserving places close a development gap?
When a government abuses its own people, who has the right to step in, and how?
After its 2010 earthquake, Haiti's aid nearly tripled in a year. Why is it still the region's poorest country?
About half of the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs above the ground. Why not bury all of it?
States promise never to use force against each other. So why do they still intervene, and at what cost?
Most of Rwanda's MPs are women, yet it is rated "Not Free". Has human rights governance there succeeded?
migration-identity-and-sovereignty: Only about one person in 27 is an international migrant. Why do some people move while most stay?
Goods and money cross borders with ease. Why is it so much harder for people?
Taiwan elects its own government. So why does it have no seat at the United Nations?
Why is India the most common country of birth, after the UK, for people living in England and Wales?
In 2014, one of Apple's Irish subsidiaries paid tax at an effective rate of 0.005% on its profits. How is that possible, and who loses?
Five countries can veto the Security Council's decisions. Can the UN still keep the world stable?
World loan and trade rules were first set in the 1940s. Do they still favour the countries that wrote them?
One treaty is healing the ozone layer. Why do so many other global environmental agreements struggle?
Seven countries claim slices of Antarctica, yet none may mine it or test weapons there. Why not?
In ten years, millions fewer people in England and Wales said they were only English. Had they really changed?
A Mini is built in Oxford by a German firm. So what does Made in Britain mean any more?

Between 1970 and 2008 the share of world trade in world GDP more than doubled. Since then it has stalled, moving between about 52% and 62% to 2024, and nationalist politics has grown. Is globalisation creating its own backlash?
globalisation-part-2: In 2024 one inflow of money into Tajikistan equalled almost half of its GDP. Which flows matter most, and for which places?
Nearly half of the world's languages are endangered, yet 4 in 10 Londoners were born abroad. Is the world becoming more alike or more diverse?
Swiss voters backed limits on immigration in 2014. What did their government actually do next?
Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
In 1990, two in three people in East Asia and the Pacific lived in extreme poverty. By 2025, fewer than 1 in 50 did. So why did the number of extremely poor people in sub-Saharan Africa rise?
Transporting the world's fruit and vegetables releases almost twice as much greenhouse gas as growing them. So is "buy local" the answer?
Shoppers pay extra for ethical labels. Do farmers, workers and the environment actually gain?
In 2016, China reported importing about 8.8 million tonnes of plastic waste. In 2018, it imported about 51,000 tonnes. What happened, and where did the waste go?
